pending_diagnosis: DIAGNOSIS: Acute Intermittent Porphyria (AIP) THE SMOKING GUN: The combination of unexplained neurovisceral symptoms (severe abdominal pain mimicking an acute abdomen with normal imaging, SIADH-induced severe hyponatremia, and rapidly progressing ascending motor neuropathy) triggered by caloric restriction and a sulfonamide, clinched by urine darkening to a port-wine color upon sunlight/air exposure. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Acute Intermittent Porphyria is an autosomal dominant metabolic disorder caused by a deficiency in hydroxymethylbilane synthase (also known as porphobilinogen deaminase), an essential intermediate enzyme in the heme biosynthesis pathway. When provoked by fasting (caloric deprivation) and porphyrogenic drugs (such as sulfonamides or CYP450 inducers), the rate-limiting enzyme ALAS1 is dramatically upregulated. This results in the massive overproduction and accumulation of neurotoxic porphyrin precursors—specifically delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) and porphobilinogen (PBG). These toxic precursors cause direct autonomic instability (tachycardia, hypertension), severe enteric autonomic neuropathy (abdominal pain, constipation), hypothalamic dysfunction causing SIADH (severe hyponatremia), central neuropsychiatric disturbances, and rapidly progressive peripheral motor axonal neuropathy.
